newsitem.title: UK: Ancient Earth once a big iceball, researchers say.
newsitem.headline: Ancient Earth once a big iceball, researchers say.

text.p: The Earth may once have been a huge "snowball," with frozen stagnant seas that warmed up only after some sort of global catastrophe, scientists said on Wednesday.

Evidence dating back 2.2 billion years shows glaciers extended to within 11 degrees of the equator -- the hot tropical zone now occupied by Angola and Mozambique, David Evans of the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena said.

Writing in the science journal Nature, he said his findings showed the ancient Earth's climate was very different from the present day -- and that the planet could, in the long run, be very resilient in the face of such great climatic change.
Evans and colleagues at Rand Afrikaans University in Johannesburg found their evidence in ancient lava beds that make up the Ongeluk Formation in South Africa.
They found polished and striated rocks and other evidence of glacial activity.

During recent ice ages, glaciers reached down from the poles only to the levels of the Ohio River Valley, present-day London and Kiev. The South African glaciers would have been at the level of present-day central America.
There is also evidence of a severe ice age between 850 and 650 million years ago.
Alan Kaufman, a geochemist at Harvard University, wrote in a commentary that the Evans study supported the idea that there was a "Snowball Earth" two billion years ago.

It would have to have been very cold for glaciers to form in the tropics, he said. "The cause of the temperature drop was probably a decline in the atmospheric level of carbon dioxide, the greenhouse gas believed to be the main regulator of Earth's climate," he wrote.
The sea would have frozen and may have gone stagnant, he added. "Covered with ice, the Earth would have reflected most of the sun's warming rays back into space," Kaufman wrote.

"Only a catastrophic event, like a huge volcanic eruption, a comet or asteroid impact, the sudden release of methane hydrates, or the overturn of a deep, stagnant ocean, could have pumped enough carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere to melt the planet's icy shell."
But the planet did recover, Evans pointed out. "Our planet's subsequent recoveries to more mild temperatures would indicate a remarkable resilience to extreme perturbation in climate," he concluded.
